bio.en: Cameron “Cam” Adams is co-founder and Chief Product Officer at Canva, the profitable design platform generating billions in ARR and growing 60%+ year over year.
bio.zh: Cameron “Cam” Adams 是 Canva 的联合创始人兼首席产品官，Canva 是一家盈利的设计平台，年经常性收入达数十亿美元，年增速超 60%。

summary.en: Cam shares how Canva stays product-obsessed at massive scale, including its freemium strategy and a unique culture where everyone has a coach and people “give away their Lego.” He discusses lessons on building MVPs, how the product team thinks about AI inside the product, and their SEO and growth strategy. The conversation also peeks into Canva's team culture and recent launches.
summary.zh: Cam 分享了 Canva 在超大规模下如何保持“产品痴迷”，包括免费增值策略，以及“人人都有教练、乐于交出手中积木”的独特文化。他讨论了打造 MVP 的教训、产品团队如何看待产品内的 AI，以及他们的 SEO 与增长策略。对话还一窥 Canva 的团队文化与近期发布。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Canva is bigger than Figma and Miro and Webflow combined. You guys are generating $2.3 billion in ARR and you're profitable. You're also growing 60% year over year and it's accelerating.
turns.zh: Canva 的规模比 Figma、Miro 和 Webflow 加起来还要大。你们一年的经常性收入就有 23 亿美元，而且还是盈利的。你们还保持着每年 60% 的增长，而且还在加速。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I run everyone through the culture of Canva. One of those sections is on giving away your Lego, finding joy in the other things of building a team, passing on your experience, helping other people do great writing or great product building or great engineering.
turns.zh: 我会带着每个人过一遍 Canva 的文化。其中有一节讲的就是“交出你的乐高”——从带团队的其他事里找到乐趣，把自己的经验传下去，帮别人写出好文章、做出好产品、写好代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When is this coaching concept? I've never heard of this.
turns.zh: 这个“教练”概念是什么时候出现的？我从来没听过。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: We don't really have managers, but everyone at Canva has a coach. They're constantly working with you to look at your skills, but also when it might be time to move on to the next level.
turns.zh: 我们其实没有传统意义上的经理，但 Canva 每个人都有一位教练。他们会持续和你一起审视你的技能，也会判断你什么时候该往下一个台阶走了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious just how you think about product management.
turns.zh: 我挺好奇的，你们是怎么看待产品经理这个角色的？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I didn't want to do product management like they did at Google, and that's because of the different cultures. I have seen product managers at other companies who are very independent of teams and that seems very weird to me. For us, product managers are really connected.
turns.zh: 我压根不想照 Google 那套来做产品管理，因为文化不一样。我也见过其他公司那种和产品团队完全脱节的产品经理，我觉得特别别扭。在咱们这儿，产品经理是深度嵌入团队的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like Canva has just been this non-stop up into the right all win, all success. In reality, that's never actually the case.
turns.zh: 给人的感觉是 Canva 一路向右上方狂飙，全是赢、全是成功。但现实显然不是这样。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: How many failure stories do you want? We got plenty.
turns.zh: 你想听多少个失败的故事？我们多的是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Today, my guest is Cameron Adams. Cameron is the co-founder and chief product officer at Canva, which is a truly incredible business and company. At the top of the episode, I share a bunch of stats. They'll probably surprise you about the scale that Canva has reached these days. (00:01:19): In our conversation, we cover a ton of ground including how Canva stays product obsessed, their freemium strategy, lessons about building MVPs, how Cam and the product team think about AI within their product, also peek into their unique team culture, their SEO and growth strategy, and also peek into some of the stuff they just launched. (00:01:37): This episode is for anyone building or growing a product or company, and I guarantee by the end of this conversation, you'll be as blown away with Canva as I am. With that, I bring you Cameron Adams. And if you enjoy this podcast, don't forget to subscribe and follow it in your favorite podcasting app or YouTube. It's the best way to avoid missing future episodes and it helps the podcast tremendously. (00:02:01): Cameron, thank you so much for being here, and welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 今天我的嘉宾是 Cameron Adams。Cameron 是 Canva 的联合创始人兼首席产品官，这是一家真正了不起的公司。在节目开头，我分享了一堆数据，关于 Canva 现在做到的规模，可能会让你大吃一惊。（00:01:19）我们的对话覆盖了很多内容，包括 Canva 如何在超大规模下依然保持“产品痴迷”、他们的免费增值策略、关于打造 MVP 的经验教训、Cam 和产品团队怎么看产品里的 AI，还聊了他们独特的团队文化、SEO 和增长策略，也提前看了一些他们刚发布的东西。（00:01:37）这期节目适合所有在做产品或做公司、想把它做大的人。我保证聊完之后，你会对 Canva 和我一样刮目相看。话不多说，有请 Cameron Adams。如果你喜欢这档播客，别忘了在喜欢的播客应用或 YouTube 上订阅关注，这是避免错过后续节目、也是对我们最大的支持。（00:02:01）Cameron，非常感谢你能来，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: It is so great to be here, Lenny. I'm very excited.
turns.zh: 能来这儿太好了，Lenny。我特别激动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm even more excited. I have at least a billion questions for you. I'm hoping I get through at least half a billion. There's so much I want to talk to you about, but I want to start with a warm and fuzzy question. Do you ever just take a moment to reflect on the insane success of this business that you've built? And before you answer that, I'm going to share some stats about Canva that I think are going to blow people's minds. So think about the answer. (00:02:30): So I was researching Canva, all of this was just... I didn't know any of this actually, and I think it'll surprise a lot of people just the scale that Canva has reached at this point. Okay. So Canva is bigger than Figma and Miro and Webflow combined both in terms of valuation and in terms of revenue. You guys are generating $2.3 billion in ARR per year and you're profitable. You've been profitable for about seven years at this point. You're also growing 60% year over year and it's accelerating, faster than last year. I think this is all quite unheard of at this scale. Do you ever just reflect back on this and, like, "Okay, I've done well."?
turns.zh: 我比你还激动。我有至少十亿个问题想问你，希望至少能问完五亿个。想聊的太多了，但我想先从一个暖场的小问题开始。你会不会偶尔停下来，回想一下自己一手打造的这门生意有多么不可思议？在你回答之前，我先分享几个关于 Canva 的数据，我觉得会惊掉大家下巴。你边听边想想答案。（00:02:30）我查 Canva 的时候，这些全都是……其实我之前一个都不知道，我想很多人也没想到 Canva 现在这个体量。好，这么说吧：不管按估值还是按收入算，Canva 都比 Figma、Miro 和 Webflow 加起来还大。你们一年的 ARR 有 23 亿美元，而且是盈利的。你们已经盈利大概七年了。你们还在以每年 60% 的速度增长，而且还在加速，比去年的增速还快。我觉得这种规模下做到这些简直闻所未闻。你会不会偶尔回过头想想，然后觉得“行吧，我干得还不错”？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: When you say it all like that, it sounds pretty amazing. I don't think every day you're cognizant of that growth and that achievement, but there are particular moments where you get to really reflect, and for me, it's most of the time when we bring the team together. Obviously now we're in a pretty virtual world, hybrid in some best cases. But when the team all get together and we celebrate is when we finally have those moments where you get to step out of yourself, look at this huge sea of people and realize what you've achieved together. (00:03:48): Probably the most recent moment we got to do that was for our 10th birthday last year. So Canva is largely centered in Australia. We've got lots of offices around the world, but we had a big birthday celebration in Sydney right on the harbor there in front of the water and we had thousands of people there, and we just got to look back on everything we've achieved over the previous 10 years, and that was the pretty amazing moment.
turns.zh: 你这么一通说完，听起来确实挺了不起的。我想平时没人会天天惦记着这个增长和成就，但有些特别的时刻，你会真正静下来反思。对我来说，大多是我们把团队聚在一起的时候。现在大家基本是远程办公，最好的情况也就是混合办公。但当整个团队聚到一起庆祝的时候，你终于能跳出自己，看着那一大片人海，意识到你们一起做到了什么。（00:03:48）最近一次大概是我们去年的十周年。Canva 的大本营在澳大利亚，全球有很多办公室，但我们在悉尼海边的港口办了一场盛大的生日庆典，几千人到场。我们回顾了这十年取得的一切，那真是一个特别震撼的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about just personally, you basically went from a designer on Google Wave to a co-founder of one of the most generational successful startups in the past decade. How does that feel?
turns.zh: 那你自己呢？你基本是从 Google Wave 的一个设计师，变成了过去十年里最成功的一批创业公司之一的联合创始人。这种感觉怎么样？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I still think I'm constantly growing, I'm constantly learning stuff. I don't feel like I've achieved a ceiling or being a massive smash hit. We're always changing how we're doing things. We're always doing things we've never done before and we feel totally like a fish out of water. So yeah, I've achieved a few things personally, but I still feel like there's so much more to go.
turns.zh: 我还是觉得自己一直在成长、一直在学新东西。我没觉得自己已经触到天花板，或者成了什么大爆款。我们一直在改变做事的方式，一直在做从没做过的事，而且经常觉得完全摸不着门道。所以，我个人是达成了一些事，但我觉得前面还有太多路要走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds right. I want to talk about the flip side from the outside, like I described, it feels like Canva has just been this non-stop up into the right all win, all success, just killing it all the time. In reality, that's never actually the case. It's often really helpful for people to hear a story of, okay, there's actually this moment of this may be all falling apart or a struggle for yourself. Is there a moment that comes to mind of just like, "Oh, man, this was really scary and hard for me."?
turns.zh: 说得对。我想聊点反面的情况。就像我前面说的，从外面看 Canva 好像一路向右上狂飙、全赢全成功，一直在碾压。可现实从来不是这样。听到“原来也有差点全盘崩掉、或者我自己特别难熬”的故事，对很多人其实很有帮助。你脑海里有没有那种“天哪，这一段真的又吓人又难”的时刻？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I think there's probably a few different stories that would resonate with your audience because there's like business kind of stories of how the actual company's tracking. There's product stories of stuff we launched that didn't go anywhere. There's team stories where you're dealing with people and all the different quirks that entails. I think I'll choose a business story. There was a moment around our 100 million valuation mark where we were putting together around... We had a lot of existing investors who were really keen to invest. This is probably our third or our fourth round by this stage, and it was all looking good. There was a particular investor who was really to lead out. We were fine with that. They were doing due diligence, got to the stage where every other investor in the round had signed on. They were super excited. They'd wired the money into our bank accounts already. They'd signed all the long docs but lead investor. (00:06:15): And about two days before they were due to sign and get all the money into our account, they came back and said, "Look, business is going great, but essentially we think we can get a better deal, so we're going to cut your valuation by 50%." It was a huge surprise and totally screwed up the entire round. All the other investors were like, "What the hell are you doing?" My co-founders, Mel and Cliff, pretty much jumped on a plane that night to go to Silicon Valley, rallied around a whole bunch of other investors, found a new lead investor, took them about a week. This was the week right before Christmas. It was incredibly stressful, incredibly tumultuous. (00:07:05): We eventually came out of it better. We actually got better terms on the deal that we came up with. That investor has fallen to the wayside now and it was a real learning moment for us in terms of how to approach fundraising and also how to be totally independent, and that's one of the reasons why we've focused on profitability for so long now. We've been profitable to spend the seven years and one of the reasons is that we never want to be put in the situation where we have to go to someone for money to ensure the survival of the business, and being profitable means that we never have to do that. We can always do it on our own terms and in our own time.
turns.zh: 我想可能有好几个不同类型的故事会引起你的听众共鸣，比如关于公司实际业务走向的，有我们发布后不了了之的产品故事，也有关于带人、处理各种人际 quirks 的团队故事。我挑一个业务相关的吧。大概在我们估值 1 亿美金的时候，我们正在推进一轮融资……已经有很多老投资人特别想跟投。这大概是我们第三或第四轮了，一切看起来都很顺利。有个投资人本来要牵头领投，我们也 ok。他们在做尽调，到这个阶段，这一轮里其他投资人全都签了，特别兴奋，钱都已经打进我们账户了，长篇文件也都签了，就差这个领投的。（00:06:15）结果在签约、钱到账的前两天，他们回来说：“你看，业务挺好，但我们觉得能拿到更好的条款，所以要把你们的估值砍掉一半。”这简直是晴天霹雳，把整轮都搞砸了。其他投资人全炸了：“你们在搞什么？”我的联合创始人 Mel 和 Cliff 当晚基本就飞去了硅谷，拉拢了一帮其他投资人，大概一周就找到了新的领投。那正好是圣诞节前一周，压力大得离谱，动荡得不行。（00:07:05）最后我们反而更好收场了。我们谈下来的条款其实更好。那个投资人现在早就被淘汰了。这对我们来说是个真正的学习时刻——关于怎么去融资，也关于怎么做到完全独立。这也是我们这么多年一直死磕盈利的原因之一。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I think one key thing is that we don't know it's very rare. We approach a board meeting just like we do anything, we craft the experience about how we think it should be and how we think it's going to be useful. So just like our board meetings or our product meetings or the way that we do launches, we have shaped that in the image that we want it to be and in the way that we think it's going to be most effective. We've always been an incredibly product-led company. We always think first and foremost about the product. That was the whole genesis of Canva itself, having a product that we thought people would love to use and desperately needed to get out into the world and that's the lens that we approach everything through. (00:11:13): In terms of board meetings, I think it's been very helpful that our financials and our growth have been amazing for so many years that we don't need to focus on it and we can just have that one slide with the graph going up and to the right. We've also attracted investors who believe in us and who understand that us driving product and getting as much product value out to our customers is probably the most important thing we can be doing. So that's why the board meetings do focus on that because what we are launching in the product, what's ahead is really determining the success of the company. Obviously, financials are important and you can do a bunch of lever pulling and thinking about margins and all that kind of stuff, but product is at the end of the day the most important thing to Canva and the thing that's going to help us stand out and continue to have success.
turns.zh: 我觉得一个关键是，我们开董事会的方式和做别的事一样——很罕见地，我们就是按我们想的去设计那个体验，设计它该是什么样、怎么才有用。所以不管是董事会、产品会，还是我们做发布的方式，我们都是按自己想要的样子、按我们认为最有效的方式来塑造的。我们一直是一家极度产品驱动的公司。我们永远先把产品放在第一位。这其实是 Canva 诞生的全部初衷——做一个我们自己觉得人们会爱用、又迫切需要推向世界的产品，我们就是用这个视角来看待一切。（00:11:13）说到董事会，因为这么多年我们的财务和增长都好得离谱，我们根本不用花精力在那上面，只要放一页“向右上走的曲线”就够了。我们也吸引了那些相信我们、明白“推动产品、把尽可能多的产品价值送到客户手里”才是我们最该做的事的投资人。所以董事会聚焦在产品上，因为我们要发布什么、接下来要做什么，才真正决定公司的成败。当然财务很重要，你也能做一堆杠杆、算利润率之类的，但说到底，产品才是 Canva 最重要的东西，才是让我们脱颖而出、持续成功的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like this point you made about how you didn't know any better almost, and it reminds me of something else I heard about Canva. It took you guys a long time to hire outside execs. Almost all your leaders are homegrown and it took you a long time to even hire outside of Australia. Its even higher in the US. Can you just talk about why that's been so important and just the impact that has come out of hiring people internally and helping people be promoted internally?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢你刚才说的——你们当时其实“什么都不懂”，这让我想起另一件关于 Canva 的事。你们花了特别久才从外面招高管。你们的 leader 几乎全是自己培养出来的，甚至连澳大利亚以外的人都招得很晚，在美国就更晚了。你能聊聊为什么这这么重要吗？内部培养人、内部提拔，带来了什么影响？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: One thing really focused on is team and culture. I think you can probably bring in the world's best person at X, Y, and Z, but if they're not fitting into your team and understanding your culture and have the same passion and vision that you do, they're not going to succeed. So it's super important that we have people along with us for the ride and that might mean everyone at Canva is awesome. They mightn't be the number one person in the world for that particular thing, but they get more done than the number one person could because they've built that trust and that safety with their team. They know how to communicate their ideas, they know how to bring other people along with them and lay out a vision in the way that we understand it at Canva, and that is a critical thing to building a great company, I think, is having that alignment across everyone, across your product teams, across your marketing teams, across your customer happiness. (00:13:21): They all need to be aligned and we all need to be rowing in the same direction. We have brought in leaders, and some of them have been incredibly successful. We have brought in leaders, and they've exited the company after a few months just because there wasn't that fit and they didn't manage to figure out or understand what Canva was and how to work within this big ecosystem. Now we've got 4,500 employees now and it's not just a matter of you coming in and bringing all your ideas. You also need to work together with all the other leaders that we have and the team that's surrounding you.
turns.zh: 我们非常聚焦的一件事就是团队和文化。我觉得你可以把全世界最牛的某方面专家请来，但如果他融不进你的团队、不理解你的文化、没有和你一样的激情和愿景，他也做不成事。所以让一群人陪你一起走这条路特别重要——这意味着 Canva 里的每个人都很厉害。他们未必是这件事上全世界第一的人，但因为和团队建立了信任和安全感，他们能比那个“第一”做成更多事。他们知道怎么表达自己的想法，知道怎么带着别人一起走，知道怎么用 Canva 的方式把愿景讲清楚。我认为打造一家好公司，关键就是让所有人——产品团队、市场团队、客户成功——都对齐。（00:13:21）大家都要对齐，朝同一个方向划。我们也引进过外部 leader，有些人特别成功。我们也引进过一些人，几个月就走了，就是因为没有契合，没搞明白 Canva 是什么、怎么在这个大生态里工作。现在我们有 4500 名员工了，已经不是你进来甩一堆想法就行的时代。你还得和所有其他 leader、你周围的团队一起协作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As a lens into what is important. Canva, when you say that they didn't understand what Canva is, what's something that doesn't click for people a lot of times that forces them to be exited potentially? What is it that's so maybe unique or important to the way you all think about stuff?
turns.zh: 作为一个看“什么重要”的视角：你说有些人“不理解 Canva 是什么”，那通常是什么东西让他们没能想通，最后可能只能走人？在你们思考事情的方式里，有什么是那么独特、那么重要的？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I have this theory that the type of product you're building very much influences the way that you think, and this stemmed out of a chat I was having with one of the product leaders at Spotify. And they said that at Spotify they do an incredible amount of talking about problems. They'll have a meeting, they'll talk about this new product feature and they'll just hash it out through conversation. And I imagined that that was because Spotify is a very auditory product. Everyone there thinks about music, sound, podcasts, that is their mindset. At Canva, we're all about visual communications. It's pitch decks, it's social media posts, it's video, it's t-shirts that you can make, and that's how we think about things in a very visual manner. (00:15:01): So one of the things that's very particular about Canva is really setting visions. And I'm in visions, not just in the sense of looking forward two, three years, but also visions in the very visual sense. We need to be able to see it. We need mock-ups. We need prototypes. You need to get that idea out of your head and present it to someone in a visual form that helps you talk about and communicate about it. That's one aspect of why some people I think don't land on their feet at Canva because they aren't necessarily visual thinkers and they don't end up communicating what they want to do in a visual way to the rest of people at Canva. (00:15:38): Another way is that the way that we've grown, the way that we've built product has been quite idiosyncratic over the years. And as I said, we've learned so much just through doing and established our own processes. And I think in any system, if someone comes up from the outside with preconceived notions or this idea that they're an expert and tries to bring that in, it's going to be rejected. So you really need to work together and I think the advice that I can give to people coming to Canva is just listen for a couple of months, figure out what is really working at Canva and why it works before you try and change it. We're very open to change and to new ideas, but just coming in wholesale and totally changing the process, just because that's what you've done somewhere else isn't going to get you the most level of success.
turns.zh: 我有个理论：你做的产品类型，会极大地影响你的思维方式。这源于我和 Spotify 一位产品 leader 的一次聊天。他说在 Spotify，他们花海量时间“聊问题”。开会的时候，他们会聊某个新产品功能，就靠对话把它聊透。我猜那是因为 Spotify 是个非常“听觉”的产品。那里每个人想的都是音乐、声音、播客，这就是他们的心智模式。而在 Canva，我们全是“视觉沟通”——PPT、社交媒体帖子、视频、你还能做 T 恤，我们就是用非常视觉化的方式思考。（00:15:01）所以 Canva 一个很特别的地方就是“设定愿景”。我说的是 vision，不只是向前看两三年，也是字面上“看得见的愿景”。我们得能看见它。我们要样机、要原型。你得把脑子里的想法拿出来，用视觉形式呈现给别人，才能聊、才能沟通。我想这就是为什么有些人在 Canva 站不住脚——因为他们未必是视觉思考者，没法用视觉的方式把自己想做的事传达给其他人。（00:15:38）另一个角度是，这些年我们成长的方式、做产品的方式都挺特别的。就像我说的，我们靠“做”学到了太多，也建立了自己的流程。我觉得任何系统里，如果有人从外面带着先入为主的观念、觉得自己是专家硬要塞进来，都会被排斥。所以你真的得一起协作。我想给来 Canva 的人的建议就是：先听几个月，搞清楚 Canva 到底什么真正管用……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes so much sense. We're talking about cultural elements and so I have one more question around culture. I saw a video interview you did once about how you love this concept of giving away your Legos, that's part of your culture and the culture at Canva broadly potentially, and this was originally popularized by Molly Graham in this first round review article. That's something you still believe in and if so, can you just describe that concept briefly because a lot of people haven't actually heard about this?
turns.zh: 太有道理了。我们一直在聊文化元素，所以我还有个关于文化的问题。我看到你之前一个视频访谈，讲到你特别喜欢“交出你的乐高”这个概念，这应该是你们文化、甚至是整个 Canva 文化的一部分。这个概念最早是 Molly Graham 在那篇 First Round 评论文章里带火的。你现在还信这个吗？如果信，能不能简单描述一下这个概念？因为很多人其实没听过。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah, Molly wrote a great article, which I actually refer everyone who joins Canva to in the cultural onboarding session, which I give them. So I run everyone through the culture at Canva and what they can expect over the next few years as they work here, and one of those sections is on giving away your Lego, and it's really important to us because part of being in a startup is scaling, when you're scaling from zero users to a million to a hundred million, and when you're scaling from three founders to 10 employees to 100 employees to 4,000 employees. You're scaling everything from the product to the internal processes you have, the finance team paying people how you deal with user feedback. Everything's just constantly growing, growing, growing. And I think this is slightly different to a traditional job where you get good at the thing that you always do and you try and turn that into a process that just continually works all the time. (00:17:58): As a startup, you just have to be changing and we want people who are flexible, you can bring new ideas, you can go to that next level. You can think about not just a million people, but 10 million people, 100 million people, a billion people using the product, and to constantly ratchet up that multiplier, you need to change yourself, which means that you probably need to give away some of the stuff that you're doing now in order to get to that next level. If you're the first email copywriter at Canva, you can get away from writing all the emails for the first year maybe, but when you're writing emails for 100 million people in 190 different countries, in 100 different languages, all at different stages of their journey through using Canva from beginners to intermediates to experts, that just massively multiplies the complexity of the job that you have to do. And if you're trying to write every single one of those emails, you have no chance of scaling. (00:18:56): So you need to think about who you're going to bring in to help you, what systems you're going to introduce, what are the processes needed to get 100 different languages translated every time you send out an email and that requires you to hand off that stuff. You need to maybe stop writing every single email, give that to someone else, be comfortable with doing that because you often build up a lot of self-identity and doing that and you get a lot of joy out of it. That's why you're a writer in the first place. But finding joy in the other things of building a team, passing on your experience, helping other people do great writing or great product building or great engineering is really what giving away your Lego is about. And we still encourage everyone to do that, to think about those moments where they need to level up in their impact, how they can bring their team along with them, how they can pass on their experience and help everyone really have a tremendous impact with the skills that they have.
turns.zh: 对，Molly 写了篇很棒的文章，我其实在文化入职环节——就是我亲自带新人的那堂课——会把所有人引去读它。我会带着每个人过一遍 Canva 的文化，以及接下来几年在这里工作能期待什么。其中有一节就是“交出你的乐高”，对我们特别重要。因为创业的一部分就是扩张——从零用户扩到一百万、一亿；从三个创始人扩到 10 人、100 人、4000 人。你的一切都在扩张：产品、内部流程、发工资的财务团队、处理用户反馈的方式。所有东西都在不停长、长、长。我觉得这和传统工作有点不一样——传统工作是把自己一直做的事做精，然后把它固化成一套永远好用的流程。（00:17:58）但作为创业公司，你只能不停变。我们要的是灵活的人，能带来新想法，能上到下一层。你要想的不只是一百万人，而是一千万、一亿、十亿人用你的产品。要不断把那个倍数拉高，你就得改变自己，也就是说，你可能得交出现在手里的一部分事，才能上到下一层。如果你是 Canva 第一个写邮件文案的人，第一年你把所有邮件都写了或许还撑得住；但当你要为一百个国家、一亿用户、一百种语言、处在不同使用阶段（从新手到进阶到专家）的人写邮件时，这件事的复杂度就爆表了。如果你想把每一封邮件都自己写，你根本不可能规模化。（00:18:56）所以你得想清楚要把活交给谁……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a lot of people and a lot of companies struggle with this idea, and I'm curious if there's something you've learned about how to actually implement this. Is it just like, "Hey, go read this article and then I might bring it up sometimes when things are changing and there's a reorg."? Or is there anything even deeper of just this is a cultural element of we are constantly giving up our Lego's giving things that we own?
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人、很多公司在“交出乐高”这件事上都很挣扎。我好奇你们有没有学到什么真正落地的方法。是就一句“去读读这篇文章，等变动、重组的时候我偶尔提一下”？还是说有更深层的东西——把它当成一种文化元素，就是我们一直在交出自己的乐高、交出我们拥有的东西？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Probably the deeper thing I think is giving people opportunity so you can talk about growth than just say, "Please grow." That's not going to be terribly effective, but giving them the opportunity and the support to do so is super important. We have a system we call coaching at Canva where you have a coach and they're constantly working with you to look at your skills, how you can improve each of those individual skills, but also what it is that you're actually doing and when it might be the time to move on to the next level. Say you are just doing a product role in this particular product and now you need to be a coach of other product managers and help build products. Understanding those pivot points is really important and our coaches help everyone at Canva. Everyone at Canva has a coach that is constantly thinking about this aspect of their personal growth. (00:21:00): And finding those opportunities where you can push someone to do something that they haven't done before or to expand upon an idea that they've had and give them ownership of that idea is super important. So when people do come to us with an amazing product idea or a feature that they want to build or an entire team that they think should be spun up, we really listen to them, and if it makes sense, we say, "Go and do that. Go and build that part of the product, grab a couple of people and start building video at Canva. Do that thing that you're talking about." And I think if you give them the opportunity and a little push to go beyond what they think they're comfortable with right now, that is the best way to drive growth in your team.
turns.zh: 我觉得更深层的做法是给人机会。你不能光说“请你成长”，那没啥用，但给他们机会和支持去成长就超级重要。我们有一套叫“教练”的体系：你有位教练，他们会持续和你一起看你的技能、看每一项怎么提升，也看你现在实际在做什么、什么时候该往上走。比如你只在一个具体产品里做产品角色，现在你需要去当其他产品经理的教练、帮他们做产品。理解这些转折点是关键，而我们的教练会帮助 Canva 里的每个人。每个人都有一个教练，一直在想他个人成长的这一面。（00:21:00）还有，去发现那些能推人去做没做过的事、或者把一个想法扩展下去、把 ownership 交给他的机会，超级重要。所以当有人带着一个超棒的产品点子、或者想做的 feature、或者想拉起一整个团队来找我们，我们真的会听；如果说得通，我们就说：“去干吧。去把产品的那块做出来，拉几个人，开始做 Canva 里的视频。就去做你说的那件事。”我觉得，给他们机会、再轻轻推一把，让他们超越现在的舒适区，是带动团队成长最好的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. There's two things I want to follow up on there. One is this coaching concept. I've never heard of this. So how does that work? Do they have a manager and they have coach, and who is this coach?
turns.zh: 好。这里面有两点我想追问。一个是“教练”这个概念，我从没听过。它到底怎么运作？他们是既有经理又有教练吗？这教练又是谁？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: We don't really have managers. So your coach is the person who thinks about you in a specialty sense. So we have specialties, engineering, product design, we got tens of different specialties across Canva, and your coach really helps.. Your coach is a similar specialty leads, so if you're a product manager, they're a product manager, so they know the skills that you have to use. They know the trajectory that you could possibly grow into. They know the structures that are around Canva that you could slot into when you want to go to the next level. And your coach constantly checks in with you, has sessions, might help you with the strategy doc, might have a one-on-one with you. They just constantly thinking about those ways that you can grow and improve at Canva. (00:22:42): And then we have probably more of a, I would say, collegiate managerial circle of colleagues who help you who do 360 feedback, all that kind of stuff. So that's the structure that we've arrived on and it's worked pretty well for us and it was driven actually by a formative coaching experience that we had as founders quite a few years ago from an external coach and we decided to bring that into Canva as a whole philosophy.
turns.zh: 我们其实没有经理。所以你的教练是从专业角度来想“你”的人。我们有各种专业线——工程、产品设计，Canva 里有几十种不同的专业线。你的教练和你是同一个专业线的负责人，所以如果你做产品，他也是做产品的，他懂你要用的那些技能，知道你未来可能成长到什么路径，也知道 Canva 里哪些结构是你上一层能嵌进去的。你的教练会持续和你 check-in、开 session、可能帮你改策略文档、可能和你一对一对聊。他们一直在琢磨你在 Canva 能怎么成长、怎么变好。（00:22:42）此外我们还有更像一个“同事管理圈”的东西，帮你做 360 度反馈之类的。这就是我们最后定型的结构，还挺好用的。它其实源于我们作为创始人多年前的一次教练体验——当时请了外部教练，然后我们决定把这套哲学整体带进 Canva。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And these coaches, are they professional coaches or they're people in the company that are like, "I will be a coach for this function."?
turns.zh: 那这些教练，是职业教练，还是公司里的人——比如“我来当这个职能的教练”？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: They're people in the company. So we've got probably close to 800 or 1,000 coaches now at Canva.
turns.zh: 是公司里的人。现在 Canva 大概有接近 800 到 1000 个教练。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: We do have very specific coaches who are just coaches and they can drop into any situation. They're not product managers, they're not designers, but they're relatively few. I think, we've got probably five of those type of coaches and they just work in very special situations, but what we're focused on is enabling the broader circle of coaches, so those 800 people to understand what it is to be a coach and have the skills of coaching. So we focus a lot on teaching them the skills of coaching, how to build a growth mindset in their coaches, all the skills that you need. So yeah, it's a massive part of Canva.
turns.zh: 确实也有一些专门的教练，只做教练，什么场景都能插进去。他们不是产品经理，也不是设计师，但人数很少。我觉得大概就五个这种类型的教练，只在很特殊的场景里工作。但我们重点放在让更广泛的教练圈子——那 800 人——真正理解“做教练”是什么意思、掌握教练的技能。所以我们花很多精力教他们教练的技能、怎么在学员身上建立成长型思维，以及所有需要的本事。所以，这真的是 Canva 很重要的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so there's a product management coach and this person helps all the PMs become better at the craft of product management.
turns.zh: 那就是说，有个“产品经理教练”，专门帮所有 PM 把产品管理这门手艺练得更好？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, so interesting. Okay, and then the performance review piece, how does that work?
turns.zh: 哇，太有意思了。好，那绩效考核这块是怎么运作的？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah. So your coach feeds into that, but we also do 360 feedback from all the people that you work with and we do that on regular cycles. As with everything at Canva, the cadence of those cycles has changed over the years, but now we do that every six months.
turns.zh: 嗯。教练会参与进去，但我们也会从所有和你共事的人那里收集 360 度反馈，而且是按固定周期做。和 Canva 所有事一样，这个周期这些年在变，但现在我们是每半年做一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We talked about product for a little bit. I want to spend a little time on product management. I'm curious just how you think about product management. There's this constant debate across tech companies about the value of PMs. Are we better with more PMs? Are there too many PMs? What do PMs do for you? You're a chief product officer. Where do you find product managers bring the most value to Canva? And then do you just have thought on the future of the field of product management?
turns.zh: 我们聊了一会儿产品，我想花点时间在产品管理上。我好奇你们怎么看产品经理。科技圈一直在争论 PM 的价值：PM 多一点好还是少一点好？PM 到底给你们带来什么？你是首席产品官，你觉得产品经理在 Canva 哪里带来的价值最大？你对这个职能的未来有什么想法？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: I don't know. It's one of those things that I don't want to quantify. I don't want to put it in a box and say this is product management. Because I've worked at a few places now. I've actually only had one real job, which was at Google where I got to experience product managers the Google way. And the way that they do product management is totally different to the way that we do it at Canva, and that's partially by design because I didn't want to do product management like they did at Google, and that's because of the different cultures that they have. Google's a fantastically engineering-driven culture and the way that they think about product management is mostly in the technical sense of like, "Here's a piece of technology, what can that technology do, how do we scale it?" At Canva, we focus a lot on experience and as I said before, it's a very visual experience, so we require a different product management process, but also a different product management mindset. (00:25:51): I think we probably did that more from the ground up than a lot of other startups just because Mel and Cliff were a lot less, I think, inculcated into how product management has done other places. I had a bit of experience from Google but was still fairly independent in my thinking, so we almost went back to first principles on how product management should be done, and to be honest, we didn't want to have the term product manager for a long, long time. It wasn't until about year '06 or '07 where we actually had product managers, we decided to cave just because it was easier to explain to people. (00:26:30): But it also took us four or five years before we even had another product owner who wasn't us. Part of that was us giving up our Lego, and I think we took a little too long to give up our Lego on that one, but the other part of it was us figuring out exactly what we wanted and how we built product and how to communicate that to someone else and get them to do it in a similar way and work with the teams in the way that we did. (00:27:00): For us, product managers are really connectives. They connect the team, ideas, data, a whole bunch of different things, and it's very messy. There's no exact recipe for how to do it, but connecting these disparate areas and moving the team and the technology and our customers to a new place, a new vision is essentially what product managers do, and it's going to involve compromise, it's going to involve changes in the feature scope, it's going to involve timelines of like, "Okay, we can't ship it in May, it's going to have to be July. Let's figure out what we can do with marketing to make that work." This constant movement and connection and reorienting around the constraints that have suddenly arisen in the last week, and that's where we see great product managers operating in Canva.
turns.zh: 我不知道。这种事我不想量化，也不想把它框死说“这就是产品管理”。因为我去过几个地方了。其实我真正只打过一份工，就是在 Google，在那里我体验了 Google 式的产品经理。他们做产品管理的方式和我们 Canva 完全不一样，这某种程度上是故意的，因为我不想照 Google 那套做，我们的文化不同。Google 是极度工程驱动的文化，他们对产品管理的理解大多偏技术层面，比如“这是一项技术，它能干嘛，怎么规模化”。而 Canva 我们非常聚焦体验，就像我之前说的，是非常视觉化的体验，所以我们需要不同的产品管理流程，也需要不同的产品管理心态。（00:25:51）我觉得我们比很多创业公司更“从零开始”，因为 Mel 和 Cliff 受其他公司产品管理那套的熏陶少得多。我虽然从 Google 带了一点经验，但思考还算独立，所以我们几乎是回到第一性原理去想产品管理该怎么做。说实话，我们很长时间都不想用“产品经理”这个头衔。直到大概 06、07 年我们才有产品经理——我们最后是妥协了，因为这样跟人解释更容易。（00:26:30）而且，我们甚至花了四五年，才出现第一个不是我们三个的产品负责人。一部分原因是我们舍不得交出乐高，这点我们确实交得有点晚了；另一部分是我们得先想清楚自己到底要什么、怎么打造产品、怎么把这套传达给别人、让他们用类似的方式做出来……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned Mel and Cliff. For folks that don't know, they're the other two co-founders of Canva and they were dating when they were starting Canva, I think it was called Fusion Books back in the day before Canva. Now, they're married. What's it like working with a married couple as the other two co-founders, and is there something they did well that didn't make you feel like this third wheel person that isn't married to them?
turns.zh: 你提到了 Mel 和 Cliff。不熟悉的人可能不知道，他们是 Canva 另外两位联合创始人，而且创业那会儿（当时公司好像还叫 Fusion Books）他们就在谈恋爱，现在结婚了。和一对已婚夫妇作为另外两位联合创始人一起工作是什么感觉？他们有没有做什么，让你不至于觉得自己是那个“局外的第三人”？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: It is always tricky working with a couple because they're on it 24/7. When you leave the office and they head home, they're still talking about product, business strategy, all the things. I think they've done a really good job of evolving those ideas overnight through the conversations they have and over dinner and walking, but then bringing that back the next day and being transparent about that and that's super important. If you are working in that kind of dynamic. There are definitely moments where I have missed out on a memo and stuff has rapidly proceeded, and I think I've just gotten used to that and gotten used to catching up really quickly, having a word with them on the side to clarify what the motivation is here and just constantly maintaining that alignment. (00:29:11): And I think it happens in any partnership or team. There's moments where there's small alignments, there's more tectonic stuff that happens over months or years, and you need to realign at some stage. I think it happens with friendships, it happens with my wife, it happens with our product teams. There's always these moments where you need to re-communicate things and relay the land of it. And I think we've been great at doing that as co-founders even for the small things and also for the more tectonic things.
turns.zh: 和一对 couple 共事总是有点 tricky，因为他们 24/7 都在聊。你下班走了，他们回家还在聊产品、聊商业策略、聊所有事。我觉得他们做得特别好的一点是，通过晚饭时、散步时的对话，把那些想法一夜之间演化出来，第二天再带回来、并且透明地同步——这一点超级重要。如果你在这种动态里工作，确实会有那么几次我漏掉了某个 memo，事情已经飞快推进了。我想我已经习惯了，习惯很快追上进度，私下跟他们确认一下“这儿的动机是什么”，然后一直维持那种对齐。（00:29:11）我觉得任何合作关系、任何团队都会这样。有些是小对齐，有些是几个月、几年才发生的“板块级”大事，你总要在某个节点重新对齐。朋友之间会这样，我和我老婆之间会这样，我们的产品团队也会这样。总有些时刻你需要重新沟通、重新说明现状。作为联合创始人，不管是小事还是大事，我们在这方面一直做得很好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This episode is brought to you by Vanta. When it comes to ensuring your company has top-notch security practices, things get complicated fast. Now, you can assess risk, secure the trust of your customers, and automate compliance for SOC 2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, and more with a single platform, Vanta. Vanta's market-leading trust management platform helps you continuously monitor compliance alongside reporting and tracking risk. Plus you can save hours by completing security questionnaires with Vanta AI. Join thousands of global companies that use Vanta to automate evidence collection, unify risk management, and streamline security reviews. Get $1,000 off Vanta when you go to vanta.com/lenny. That's V-A-N-T-A.com/lenny. (00:30:37): I'm going to go back to the beginning of Canva. I know that it took you guys a year of building before you launched it, so it took you a year to build the MVP essentially. And I know you have some strong opinions on how long to wait, how MVPs are often way too early. Can you talk about that just why you guys waited so long before launching clearly worked out and so I'm just curious your lessons from that experience.
turns.zh: 本期节目由 Vanta 赞助。说到确保公司有一流的安全实践，事情很快就会变复杂。现在你可以用 Vanta 这一个平台来评估风险、赢得客户信任，并自动化完成 SOC 2、ISO 27001、HIPAA 等合规。Vanta 这个业界领先的可信管理平台，帮你持续监控合规、做报表、追踪风险。而且用 Vanta AI 填安全问卷能省下大把时间。加入成千上万家使用 Vanta 的公司，让证据收集自动化、统一风险管理、简化安全审查。去 vanta.com/lenny 能省 1000 美元。就是 V-A-N-T-A.com/lenny。（00:30:37）我想回到 Canva 最早的时候。我知道你们花了一年才把它做出来发布，也就是本质上花了一年才做出 MVP。而且我知道你对“要等多久、MVP 常常太早”有很鲜明的观点。你能聊聊为什么你们等了那么久才发布——显然结果很好——我就好奇你从那段经历里学到了什么。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah, so when we launched or when we were building the Lean Startup book came out, so that was all anyone talked to us about investors, other people building products, trying to give us advice. They were like, "Just get something out the door, as crappy as it is just to get in front of users." I think, for us, the product is the experience and giving people a great experience is an intrinsic part of the product. It's also an intrinsic part of how we've grown. People having a good experience of being enthusiastic about it has been how we've spread the word of Canva and organic word-of-mouth growth was the biggest driver of Canva's growth for many years and probably still is, I think. People just telling someone else to jump on this amazing product, I don't think we would've had that if we just put our pretty crappy product that people didn't have joy in using. Sure, it might've got the job done, but if they weren't excited about using it the next day, then that wasn't a bar that we wanted to hit. (00:32:08): So we did hold off on launching the product for a long time and investors did ask us many, many times, "When are you launching? Can you just get this thing out the door?" But we had done enough research, we knew the problem space, we knew what people wanted from the product. Part of that was due to the work that Mel and Cliff did on Fusion Books in a very constrained area. They had looked at school yearbooks, they had built an experience for that, and they had observed what worked didn't work and how they might scale that into a bigger product. It also worked for me who'd worked in a lot of creative tools and built a lot of creative tools over the previous 15 years. So I had a lot of understanding of how people interacted with these systems and the experience that we wanted to build. (00:32:57): So we did hold off and the product we launched launched, we obviously weren't happy with. You have to launch something that you're not completely happy with, all the rough edges, but you're releasing it knowing that the rough edges are going to be outweighed by the joyful experience. We still did a ton of user testing, right? It's not like we just launched this thing blind and said, "We hope people like it." We did a ton of user testing. We did a ton of user research into the features that people wanted, and we built that up over time. And one year to me actually seems like short time, a lot of people think it's a long time, but one year was just enough for us to scrape in with an experience that people did truly love when we launched, and particularly the market that we went after when we launched really loved it.
turns.zh: 对，我们构建、发布那会儿，《精益创业》刚出，所以所有投资人、其他做产品的人、想给我们建议的人，开口都是那套。他们会说：“赶紧弄个东西上线，多烂都行，先跑到用户面前。”我觉得对我们来说，产品就是体验，给人好的体验是产品内在的一部分，也是我们成长的内在一部分。人们用得开心、充满热情，这就是 Canva 口碑传播的方式——很多年里，有机的口碑增长是 Canva 增长最大的驱动力，我觉得现在可能也是。人们就只是跟别人说“去用这个超棒的产品”。如果当时我们丢出一个大家都用得不爽的半成品，我觉得不会有这种效果。当然，它也许能完成任务，但如果他们第二天不想再用，那不是我们想达到的及格线。（00:32:08）所以我们确实拖了很久才发布。投资人也问了我们无数次：“你们到底什么时候发？能不能先把这东西弄出去？”但我们做了足够的调研，我们懂这个问题空间，懂人们想要什么。一部分是因为 Mel 和 Cliff 在 Fusion Books 那个很垂直的场景里做的功课。他们研究过学校年鉴，为那个场景做过一套体验，也观察过什么管用、什么不管用、怎么把它放大成一个更大的产品。这对我也有用——我之前做过很多创意工具，15 年里打造过不少。所以我很懂人们怎么和这些系统交互，也懂我们想打造的体验。（00:32:57）所以我们确实拖了。而我们发布的那版，我们显然也不满意。你必须发布一个你并不完全满意的东西……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious just what advice you share with founders when they're asking you how joyous does this first version have to be? How awesome does my MVP need to be? One thread I picked up as you were describing your experiences, you all had deep experience in this space, so you knew what you wanted to build. It wasn't like this dark forest of exploration is like we know what we want generally. Do you have advice you share with founders of how awesome their MVP should be and when it's worth spending a year or two or three building it?
turns.zh: 我好奇的是，当创始人问你“第一版得让人多快乐”“我的 MVP 得有多棒”时，你给他们什么建议？我听你讲经历时抓到一条线索：你们在那个领域都有很深的经验，所以你们知道自己想造什么，不是在一片黑暗森林里瞎探索。你会给创始人什么建议——MVP 得有多棒，什么时候值得花一两年、甚至三年去打造它？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: There's a couple of points in there. First is that even today we build for ourselves, and I think this is advice that probably a lot of product people wouldn't give you is that you shouldn't build for yourself, you should build for your customer. But I think we're fortunate that we are our customer and that the problems we experience are the problems that hundreds of millions, billions of people experience. I think that is maybe a fortunate part of just the problem area that we're interested in, but it has enabled us to move really quickly on the product because we can quickly know what's working in the product, whether this feature is useful, whether it's reached that bar of a great experience. (00:35:03): So that's one aspect of it and I think that is also about being passionate, you entering an area that you are extremely passionate about. I often hear people are like, "I want to do a tech startup. What is the best area I should focus on to build a product in?" And to me, that is totally the wrong way to go about building a company that you're going to spend the next 10, 20 years in because if you're in an area that you are particularly passionate about but you see the opportunity to make a bit of money or have some external measure of success, that is a terrible way to go about being a founder because you're going to hit these rock bottom dark places and if the passion isn't driving you through that, you're going to have an incredibly hard time getting to the next step. So that's probably the first area I talk about in terms of knowing when a product is amazing. (00:35:58): The second one is that it really needs to spark, joy, and delight in people and just pure excitement. It can't just be like, "Oh, yeah, this is a useful tool for me." It needs to light up their eyes. They need to be like, "How do I sign up for this thing tomorrow? How do I get it? How do I pay for it?" And they need to want to talk to other people about it because in the early days of your startup, you don't have marketing dollars, you don't have channels which you can go to immediately get access to a million people. You need to really foster the first people that are going to use your product and they're going to be the ones that are going to spread it and they're going to set the foundations for your growth.
turns.zh: 这里有几层意思。第一，直到今天我们都为自己而做。我觉得这条建议很多产品人可能不会给你——他们告诉你要为客户做、别为自己做。但我觉得我们很幸运，我们自己就是客户，我们遇到的问题就是几亿、几十亿人遇到的问题。我想这大概是因为我们感兴趣的问题领域碰巧如此，但它让我们在产品上能跑得飞快，因为我们能立刻知道什么管用、这个 feature 有用没用、有没有达到“好体验”的线。（00:35:03）这是一方面，另一方面也是关于激情——进入一个你极度热爱的领域。我经常听到有人说：“我想做个科技创业。我该聚焦哪个领域最好？”对我来说，这完全是错的方向。如果你在一个自己特别有激情、但也看到赚钱机会或有外界成功标准的领域，那做 founder 会非常痛苦，因为你一定会跌到谷底、跌进黑暗里，如果激情不能带你熬过去，你很难走到下一步。所以关于“怎么算一个牛产品”，这是我首先聊的。（00:35:58）第二点是，它真的得能点燃人们的 joy 和 delight，就是纯粹的兴奋。不能只是“哦对，这是个对我有用的工具”。它得让人眼睛发亮。他们得是“我明天怎么注册？怎么拿到？怎么付费？”而且他们得想跟别人聊它，因为早期……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So piece of advice number one is work on something you really want yourself that you're excited to work on. Two is get it to a place where it lights up people's eyes. They're just so excited with this thing. For that second bar, what was it for Canva? Was it just that it was impossible to do this design in a browser?
turns.zh: 有意思。所以第一条建议是：做你真正自己想要、自己兴奋去做的事。第二条是：把它做到让人眼睛发亮，人们对它超级兴奋。那第二条，对 Canva 来说是什么？是因为在浏览器里根本做不了这种设计吗？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: It was 2012, 2013 when we launched and visual content was still in its infancy. Instagram had only been out a couple of years. Pinterest was on the rise. People were just getting used to creating visuals and it was hived off to a very select few because to create those visuals you needed to afford some expensive software, know how to use that expensive software, nowhere to go to get fonts and photos and illustrations, know how to put that together into something that looked decent and then ship that off. It was something that only 1% of the world could do and democratizing design, empowering the world to design is Canva's entire mission, and we saw this sweet spot at the time in social media. It wasn't what we set out to go after. We set out to democratize design to bring design to literally everyone in the world and to everything that they're doing. (00:37:59): But through the user testing that we did, through the levels of excitement that we saw from different people, social media managers really came to the fore at that time. So we knew that they really fit what we could ship right now. We didn't ship a presentation product or a T-shirt builder in our very first version. We shipped a thing that could make square landscape and portrait graphics and blog post graphics, and that got a particular segment of society excited. We added on all the things afterwards because that was part of vision and ultimately what we wanted to build. But with a team of 10 people in the space of a year, building something that really got social media managers excited was what we could pull off. And that's something we realized in the last six months of that launch year. We didn't quite know who our audience was going to be. We knew it was a tool that anyone could use, but in that last six months of user testing and refining is when we really identified that first target market and we just leant into it.
turns.zh: 我们发布是 2012、2013 年，视觉内容还在起步期。Instagram 才出来一两年。Pinterest 在起来。人们刚开始习惯做视觉内容，而且这被圈在极少数人手里——因为要做那些视觉内容，你得买得起贵的软件、得会用、得知道去哪弄字体图片插画、得知道怎么拼出像样的东西再发出去。全世界只有 1% 的人能做。而“让设计民主化、让全世界都能设计”正是 Canva 整个使命，我们在社交媒体上看到了那个甜蜜点。那不是我们一开始瞄准的。我们出发是要把设计带给全世界的每一个人、带到他们做的每件事里。（00:37:59）但通过用户测试、通过我们看到不同人表现出的兴奋度，社交媒体运营者当时真的冲到了最前面。所以我们知道他们正好适配我们现在能交付的东西。第一版里我们没发演示文稿产品，也没发 T 恤 builder。我们发的是能做出方形、横版、竖版图形和博客配图的东西，它让社会上某一群人兴奋了。其他所有东西都是后来加的，因为那本来就是愿景、是我们最终想造的。但一个 10 人的团队，在一年时间里，做出真正让社交媒体运营者兴奋的东西，那是我们能做到的。而那是我们在这个发布年的最后六个月才意识到的。我们之前不太确定受众是谁。我们知道这是个谁都能用的工具，但在那最后六个月的用户测试和调整里，我们才真正锁定第一个目标市场，然后全力扑上去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many things you all nailed early on. One of them is the focus persona/ICP, which is you said social media managers. Just to take the lesson from that, you basically saw that segment getting the most excited about the product and that told you, let's focus on this group. Is that right?
turns.zh: 你们早期搞定的东西太多了。其中一个就是聚焦的 persona/ICP，也就是你说的社交媒体运营者。就按那个经验来说，你基本是看到这群人对产品最兴奋，于是就告诉自己“聚焦这群人”。对吗？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And was it like an order magnitude more excited? What do people look for there that tells them, "This is the one."? What did you see there other than just more excitement?
turns.zh: 那是说兴奋度高了一个数量级？人们会看什么信号来判断“就是它了”？除了更兴奋，你还看到了什么？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: It was just incredibly emotive language, like sheer joy. Particularly coming into the product, we worked a lot on the onboarding process in the last couple of months of launch and that was really pivotal because the product features were there. You could add text, you could add images, you can change the color of things, you can move stuff around the page. It was a simple but powerful product, but there was this thing holding people back from actually using it and understanding what Canva could do for them. And when user tested the onboarding of Canva a ton, actually usertesting.com had just launched them, which really unlocked us because we didn't have to do these big formal labs or anything like that. We could just go online and get results in the space of half an hour. So that was like a pivotal unlock for our product process and that's something we still employ today. (00:40:39): And through that, we tailored the onboarding process to get people excited and to understand the deeper goal with Canva and the deeper impact it could let them have. It wasn't just about letting them put a pretty picture on the page, it really unlocked their ideas and let them do things they couldn't do before. And we shaped the onboarding to do that and it resonated the most with social media managers because they had this massive content need that they couldn't really service. And in the first minute of Canva with the right onboarding, it just unlocked the whole realm of productivity and impact that they didn't have before and that's why they got super excited.
turns.zh: 就是极度情绪化的语言，那种纯粹的 joy。特别是进产品的时候，我们在发布前最后几个月狠下了功夫做 onboarding，那非常关键，因为功能都在那儿了——能加文字、能加图、能改颜色、能在页面上挪东西。是个简单但强大的产品，但有个东西在拦着人真正用它、理解 Canva 能给他们什么。我们当时做了大量 onboarding 的用户测试，其实 usertesting.com 刚上线，这真的帮了我们，因为我们不用搞那些正式的大实验室了，上网半小时就能拿到结果。这对我们的产品流程是个关键解锁，到现在还在用。（00:40:39）通过它，我们把 onboarding 打磨成能让人兴奋、能让他们理解 Canva 更深层的目标和更深层的影响。不是只让他们在页面上放张好看的图，而是真的打开他们的想法，让他们做出以前做不到的事。我们就是照这个来设计 onboarding 的，而它最能引起共鸣的正是社交媒体运营者——他们有巨大的内容需求却满足不了。在 Canva 的第一分钟里，配合对的 onboarding，直接就解锁了他们以前没有的生产力和影响力，这就是他们超级兴奋的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We talk a lot on this podcast about the power of onboarding and the impact that can have on retention and everything down funnel. Do you remember what the unlock was in terms of and getting more people activated? Is there anything that's something that other people can learn from?
turns.zh: 我们这档播客聊过很多 onboarding 的威力，以及它对留存、对漏斗下游一切的影响。你还记得那个“解锁点”是什么吗、怎么让更多人激活？有没有别人能借鉴的？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: For us, it was taking that first step, particularly with Canva and any I think creative tool. There's a real fear of the blank page. So prior to any onboarding thought from us, we had a blank page. We had a few coach marks that said, "Here's where you do this, here's where you do this." And then they'd be left on this blank page and people would freak out. So what we really focused on was just taking that first step and then the next step and then the next step. And before they knew it, they built a design. And the way that we did that was to encourage a really simple step. So the first one was click on this search box and search for a monkey. It literally said that. (00:42:18): Searching for a monkey is something you probably don't do in most tools. So it was a little surprising, which was a good inroad, but it was still super easy. Anyone can type monkey. And then you type that in, it comes up with this whole sway the monkey images, which look hilarious, and just dragging one of those out onto a page is another simple step. And we just got people to walk through that keeping their interest up, keeping the bar of effort quite low, but within three or four steps, they'd built up something that they'd never been able to do before, and it surprised them. The words that we literally got out of years at testing were, I didn't know I could be a designer. And that was what we managed to do through several rounds of refinement on the onboarding process. It is lowering the barriers to entry and also increasing the amount of delight, and I think those two things are what you should be aiming for with your onboarding.
turns.zh: 对我们来说，是迈出的第一步，尤其是 Canva 这种、我觉得任何创意工具都这样。人们真的怕“空白页”。所以在我们任何 onboarding 想法之前，我们给的是一张空白页，加几个小提示“这儿做这个、那儿做这个”，然后就把人留在空白页上，大家就慌了。所以我们聚焦的就是：先迈第一步，然后下一步、再下一步。等他们回过神，已经做出一个设计了。我们的做法是鼓励一个超简单的步骤：第一步，点这个搜索框，搜一只猴子。字面意思就是这么写的。（00:42:18）搜猴子大概不是大多数工具里你会做的事，所以有点意外，是个不错的切入，但又特别简单，谁都能打“猴子”。你打进去，出来一堆猴子的图，看着特别逗，把其中一张拖到页面上，又是一步简单的操作。我们就这么带着人走，一直吊着他们的兴趣，把每一步的门槛压得很低，但三四步之内，他们就做出了以前从没做出来的东西，连他们自己都惊讶。我们做了好几轮打磨后，从测试里听到的原话是：“我不知道我也能当设计师。”这就是我们通过好几轮 onboarding 优化做到的——降低进入门槛，同时提升 delight，我觉得这两点就是你做 onboarding 该瞄准的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an incredible insight. Is there a video of that original onboarding out there or is the current one still similar?
turns.zh: 这洞察太牛了。那个最初的 onboarding 有视频流传吗？还是说现在的版本还差不多？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: The current one isn't similar. We have constantly gone back to it because it performs really well. We do actually apply the same approach of little steps building up into bigger accomplishments, and that's actually rolled out through our last round of launches for the last couple of years through something we call learn and play. So with every launch that we do now, we think about how to teach people about that feature and how to get them really involved in it. We have a whole series of learn and plays where when we launch AI photo editing, they can try it out right then and there. They've got some great content that they can immediately operate on, and it's a super simple step for them to type in a prompt and see the result of that.
turns.zh: 现在的已经不像了。但我们一直回头改它，因为它表现太好了。我们确实还在用“小步累积成大成就”的那套方法，而且这两年通过我们叫“learn and play”的东西，已经铺到了最近几轮发布里。现在我们每次发布，都会想怎么教用户用这个功能、怎么让他们真正参与进来。我们有一整套 learn and play：比如发布 AI 修图时，他们当场就能试，有现成的好内容可以马上操作，对他们来说，打一句 prompt 看结果就是超简单的一步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think an interesting and really important takeaway here is you built a very delightful, incredible, innovative product, but it still didn't work until you figured out the onboarding and that you needed to figure out the persona to focus on. All those things end up being incredibly important, it's not just build something amazing and delightful.
turns.zh: 我觉得这里有个有趣也特别重要的收获：你们做出了一个超 delight、超牛、超创新的产品，但在你们搞懂 onboarding、搞懂该聚焦哪个 persona 之前，它还是不行。所有这些事最后都极其重要，不是“做个超棒超 delight 的东西”就完了。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Definitely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Staying within this realm of growth, you've grown in large part thanks to this incredibly SEO template strategy. You mentioned in interview there's this guy, Andre that came on early and helped you figure this stuff out. Is that true? And if so, what was the key insight that he had that led to such a great success in terms of growth for you all?
turns.zh: 还是在增长这个话题里，你们很大程度上靠的是那个超厉害的 SEO 模板策略。你之前采访里提到一个叫 Andre 的人，很早就加入了，帮你们搞明白这些。是真的吗？如果是，他有什么关键洞察，让你们在增长上取得这么大的成功？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Andre is an amazing guy. He's actually been in and out of Canva three or four times now.
turns.zh: Andre 是个牛人。其实他进进出出 Canva 已经三四次了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Keep pulling him back.
turns.zh: 一直把他拉回来。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah, keep pulling him back. We originally found him, he came from a startup that was going under here in Sydney. We had thought about SEO. We knew it was this thing that you could use, and I think in a couple of our pitch decks, we had SEO as a whole growth channel that we were going to execute upon in order for investors to make a ton of money, but we pretty much knew nothing about it. And it was sitting away in our backlog of things to do in the first couple of years of Canva. And we came across Andre and he just really crystallized what SEO was and how it would actually help us grow. So we brought him on, he rolled out his strategy and it was fantastically effective. It was also incredibly cheap, and it was super easy for us to do ourselves. (00:45:51): He set up a whole team of people who looked at people's motivations and the top jobs to be done that Canva could service. He then mapped that through the entire experience of going into Google, typing a search query, getting that search query, seeing that it was a great result, firstly getting to the top result, but then also the experience after they landed on Canva. So if they searched for want to make a Halloween poster, the top Google result would be Canva. They'd click on it, they'd land on the Halloween poster landing page. It would tell them how they were going to do, it show you how the product was going to do that, have a button there that immediately took them into a Halloween poster template, went through a fantastic onboarding of customizing that poster really simply, and then they would hit done, download the image, and they had a fantastic experience and he thought through that whole end-to-end flow from first landing on Google and typing into the search box through to that magic moment where they're like, "Canva just helped me do something amazing and I want to do it again."
turns.zh: 对，一直拉他回来。我们最早找到他时，他来自悉尼一家快撑不下去的创业公司。我们之前想过 SEO，知道这是个能用的东西，我想我们好几版融资 PPT 里都把它当成一条完整的增长渠道，说要让投资人赚翻，但其实我们基本啥也不懂。它在 Canva 头两年的待办清单里一直躺在那儿。然后我们碰到了 Andre，他把 SEO 到底是什么、它到底怎么帮我们增长，一下子讲透了。所以我们把他拉进来，他推开了他的策略，效果好得离谱。而且特别便宜，我们自己做起也超简单。（00:45:51）他搭了一整支团队，去研究人们的动机、Canva 能解决的最重要的“待办任务”。然后他把整条体验都画了出来：进 Google、打搜索词、匹配到那个词、先做到排第一，再到他们落到 Canva 之后的体验。比如他们搜“想做个万圣节海报”，Google 第一条就是 Canva。他们点进去，落到万圣节海报落地页，页面告诉他们怎么做、展示产品会怎么做，还有一个按钮直接把他们带进万圣节海报模板，经过特别顺畅的 onboarding 简单定制，然后点完成、下载图片，得到超棒的体验。他把从第一次落在 Google、打进搜索框，到那个“Canva 刚帮我做了件超棒的事、我还想再做”的魔法时刻，整条端到端流程都想透了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. So a few things I'm hearing there. One is figure out the jobs to be done of potential users, figuring out where their search volume, figure out ones you can actually solve for them, like say a Halloween poster, and then think about that experience end to end from search to landing. And obviously, you have to deliver on that promise. You have to actually show them a really cool Halloween poster that they can create, right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，我听到几点。一是搞清楚潜在用户的“待办任务”，搞清楚哪里的搜索量大，搞清楚你真正能帮他们解决的——比如万圣节海报——然后从搜索到落地，把体验想通端到端。而且显然你得兑现承诺，得真的给他们看到一个超酷的、能做的万圣节海报，对吧？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah. Again, it's like product led truly means product led because you can't just SEO the hell out of something that is a terrible experience. So tying that experience at the end of the SEO journey is just as important as the technicalities of SEO itself, and Andre really harnessed the whole spectrum of that to produce the end experience, which ultimately ended up with an active user having a delightful experience.
turns.zh: 对。再说一遍，产品驱动真正意味着产品驱动，因为你不能把一个体验很烂的东西靠 SEO 硬推。所以把体验接在 SEO 旅程的末端，和 SEO 本身的技术细节一样重要。Andre 真正把整个光谱都用上了，最后交付的是一个活跃用户拿到 delight 体验的结局。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else along those lines that was really surprising to you or really, wow, that worked a lot better than I thought because it's probably one of the most well executed, most successful SEO strategies in history. And I'm so curious, just if there's anything else there that's just like, "Oh, wow, that was really effective and I didn't expect that."
turns.zh: 在那条线上，还有什么让你特别意外、或者“哇，比我想的好用太多了”的？因为这大概是史上执行得最到位、最成功的 SEO 策略之一。我特别好奇，还有没有别的东西是“哇，真的太有效了，我没想到”的？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: There's a ton in the SEO realm that Andre drove that can get quite technical. But I think one of the other pivotal growth moments for us was internationalization. I think as an Australian company, we're fortunate in that Australia isn't a great market to focus on. We've got 25 million people here. It's okay, but it's not sizeable. It's not going to make you a huge success. Whereas probably a startup that starts in the US will tend to focus on the US because it's a huge monetizable market, and you can entirely create a great company that just services the US. But from Australia, we needed to think about the world. And that meant that we very quickly got into internationalization. (00:48:52): We started localizing and internationalizing our products three years after launch, which is quite early compared to a lot of other companies. And we tackled it with real vigor. We had a goal of being in five different languages within the first year of localization, and we actually hit eight in that first year. And then we set ourselves a goal of being in 100 different languages the next year. And the internationalization team smashed that goal by the end of 2017. And it has drastically changed Canva's growth trajectory because being in other languages, offering a localized experience, something that people in Brazil or Indonesia or Spain or Poland can authentically feel like they're using a product that's made for them has totally changed who our market is, how quickly we can grow. And the way the product's used internationalizing into Brazilian Portuguese meant that we had to focus a ton more on the Android mobile experience, which was really different for us because we focused a lot on the desktop experience for the first four years. (00:49:58): People also in Brazil run entire businesses from their mobile phone and the types of content they're creating to interact with their audience is totally different. So it's actually shaped our product and changed our product trajectory as a result of thinking about internationalization. And it has just fueled tremendous growth. Brazil, India, Indonesia, they're all in our top five markets and they grow way faster than the US does.
turns.zh: SEO 领域 Andre 推动的、能讲到很技术的事有一大堆。但我觉得我们另一个关键的增长时刻是国际化。作为一家澳大利亚公司，我们挺幸运——澳大利亚不是个好聚焦的市场，这里只有 2500 万人，还行，但不大，撑不起巨大的成功。而一家从美国起步的创业公司，往往会聚焦美国，因为它是个能变现的大市场，你完全可以只服务美国就做成一家好公司。但从澳大利亚出发，我们得想全世界。这意味着我们很早就做国际化了。（00:48:52）我们发布三年后就开始本地化、国际化，比很多公司都早。而且我们干得很猛。我们的目标是在本地化第一年覆盖五种语言，结果第一年就做到了八种。第二年我们定了覆盖 100 种语言的目标。国际化团队在 2017 年底前狠狠超额完成了。这彻底改变了 Canva 的增长轨迹，因为用别的语言、提供本地化体验——让巴西、印尼、西班牙、波兰的人真觉得这是为他们做的产品——彻底改变了我们的市场是谁、我们能长多快。而产品用巴西葡语国际化，意味着我们得把 Android 移动端体验大幅加强，这对我们很不一样，因为前四年我们主要聚焦桌面端。（00:49:58）巴西人很多是用手机经营整个生意的，他们为触达受众而做的内容类型也完全不一样。所以这其实塑造了我们的产品、改变了我们的产品……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you went international in your four, something like that, which is really early for a company. It also makes sense for SEO plus internationalization. Makes tons of sense.
turns.zh: 我知道你们大概第四年就开始国际化了，对一家公司来说真的很早。而且 SEO 加上国际化，逻辑上完全说得通。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 完全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's a lot more surface area. Okay. I'm going to have two more questions. One is around your freemium strategy. Another a thing you all nailed. There's just this, you're both seeing incredible growth and incredible monetization. I'm curious what your philosophy is on what to include in the free plan versus what people should pay for because it's clearly worked out great.
turns.zh: 那覆盖面就大多了。好，我还有两个问题。一个是你们的免费增值策略——你们另一个搞定的东西。你们一边增长惊人，一边变现也惊人。我好奇你们的哲学是：免费版里放什么、什么该让人付费，因为结果显然好得不得了。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Freemium for us wasn't so much a growth strategy or a monetization strategy as much as it spoke to our core mission of empowering the world to design. We truly want to democratize design, which means we want to get design into the hands of as many people as we can because we think that the world is a better place when more people can create really rich visual content. So freemium just made sense to us because we could get the tool into billions of people's hands and they wouldn't necessarily have to pay for it. And much of the world can't pay for products because they just don't have access to that level of income. (00:51:36): So providing that equality was really important to us. But also you need to build a viable business because you can't help the world design if you can't afford to keep the lights on. So freemium just really hit this sweet spot for us between philosophy and business building, so it was always part of our plan since day one. We initially had element sales as our business models. So when we first went to pitch Canva, it was all about create a design. Anything you use in that design will cost you a dollar. So if you dragged in a monkey and you wanted to export that whole design, you'd have to pay a dollar for the money.
turns.zh: 对我们来说，免费增值与其说是增长策略或变现策略，不如说它呼应了我们的核心使命——让全世界都能设计。我们真心想让设计民主化，意思是想把它交到尽可能多的人手里，因为我们认为，当更多人能创造丰富的视觉内容时，世界会更好。所以免费增值对我们就是顺理成章——我们能把这个工具交到几十亿人手里，他们不一定要付钱。而且世界上很多人根本付不起，因为他们没有那个收入水平。（00:51:36）所以提供这种平等对我们很重要。但你同时也得做一门能活下去的生意，因为如果连灯都开不起，你也没法帮世界设计。所以免费增值正好击中了我们的甜点——哲学和做生意之间，所以从第一天起它就是我们计划的一部分。我们最初的业务模型是卖素材。最早去 pitch Canva 时，讲的全是“做设计。设计里你用的任何东西收你一美元”。所以你拖进一只猴子、想导出整个设计，就得为那只猴子付一美元。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I've done that many times.
turns.zh: 对，我这么干过好多次。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yes. It was really exciting to investors at the time. It was also really exciting to the content creators who were giving us the monkeys to put into our product. It was a totally new business model. It unlocked, I think, an area that a lot of people were unfamiliar with, which was stock photography. Most people had not paid 100, $500 for photo, and that really held them back from being visual content creators. So it was a really unique innovation for us. And for the first two years of Canva's life, that was how we derived our revenue. It grew pretty well. It was still like, I don't know, 30% month-on-month growth in terms of revenue. But you can do that in the early stages of a startup. It wasn't until we introduced our first subscription product that we saw really hockey stick growth in our revenue. And that was always the plan to launch a subscription product. (00:53:09): But as with many things, it was a vision that we didn't quite have meat around the bones. So we knew we wanted to put in a subscription what exactly that subscription would look like. We didn't quite know. And through the first couple of years of Canva, we started noticing what people were asking for, what they would be more likely to pay in a subscription for. And that formed the first few features that became what was then called Canva for Work, which is now called Canva Pro. And we launched our first subscription, I think about three years after we launched the first product, and we just rapidly saw the revenue from the subscription start overtaking the $1 image payments. (00:53:53): So much so that three or four years later we made image element payments part of the subscription. And again, that was like a second hockey stick in gross in terms of the revenue from the subscription because all you can eat images inside the Canva Pro subscription with just amazing value add for people. And I don't even know if we get any revenue from image element sales now. It's all about just going into this subscription.
turns.zh: 对。当时投资人特别兴奋。那些把猴子放进我们产品的素材创作者也特别兴奋。这是个全新的商业模式。它打开了，我觉得，很多人不熟悉的一个领域——图库照片。大多数人从没花 100、500 美元买过照片，而这真的挡住了他们成为视觉内容创作者。所以对我们来说这是个很独特的创新。在 Canva 头两年，我们就是靠这个收入的，长得还不错，大概每月 30% 的环比增长吧，但创业早期能这样。直到我们推出第一个订阅产品，收入才真正出现曲棍球杆式的增长。而推订阅本来就在计划里。（00:53:09）但和很多事一样，那是个我们还没想清楚的愿景。我们知道想做订阅，但具体长什么样，不太确定。在 Canva 头几年，我们开始注意到人们想要什么、更可能为什么付订阅费。这就形成了最早几个功能，当时叫 Canva for Work，现在叫 Canva Pro。我们在第一个产品发布大概三年后推出第一个订阅，立刻就看到订阅收入开始超过那一美元买图的钱。（00:53:53）以至于三四年之后，我们把素材付费并进了订阅里。这又带来第二根曲棍球杆——Canva Pro 订阅里“图片随便用”，对人们来说是超值的加成。我现在甚至不知道素材付费还能不能带来收入，反正都变成……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Just hockey stick after hockey sticks. Speaking of another hockey stick, I want to talk about AI.
turns.zh: 太牛了。曲棍球杆接二连三。说到另一根曲棍球杆，我想聊 AI。

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Oh, a whole hockey team of hockey sticks.
turns.zh: 哦，是一整支曲棍球队的曲棍球杆。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just need to acquire hockey teams. I want to talk about AI, something on the top of everyone's minds these days. It's another area you guys have nailed. You're doing amazing work with AI. It's providing actual value and business impact. I hear you have an amazing internal AI ops team. Is there anything that you've learned so far that you can share about just how to integrate AI successfully and effectively into a product?
turns.zh: 只需要去收购曲棍球队了。我想聊 AI，这是最近 everyone 都在想的事。这也是你们搞定的另一个领域。你们在 AI 上做得超棒，带来了真实的价值和业务影响。我听说你们有个超厉害的内部 AI 运营团队。到目前为止你学到、能分享的，关于怎么把 AI 成功有效地整合进产品，有什么？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: As a technology company, you always just need to be constantly evolving and using the best technology. And when we started that was mobile phones and cloud computing. They were the innovations that came in that really unlocked Canva. AI is the next decade I think of innovation. It's the next pivotal piece of technology that helps you build better products, but it also can't just be the basis for your product. You can't just be a product that's purely built on AI on being a rapper around an LLM or something like that. You still need to think about what it is that people want to do and how you build a product that actually meets that need. It isn't just about slapping a chatbot on something that already existed. It's about deeply thinking about how AI can help them get to that goal even faster. And we view AI as the next way of democratizing design and empowering the world to design, helping more people design, helping more people design quicker, helping more people design quicker with better quality. And that's how we approach every aspect of including AI in the Canva platform. (00:56:04): We've had a team of machine learning engineers for probably seven years now. I think their work has become a lot more visual now and more customer facing way back when they were just doing recommendation engines inside our emails and our homepage and suggesting templates to you. But now they get to work with some really cool technology, which lets them produce images for people and create designs and summarize text and translate to a hundred different languages like it's really stuff that you can put directly in front of customers now, and that's super exciting. And over the last couple of years, we've built up more and more visual AI experts inside Canva, and we approach AI inside the product through three pillars. (00:56:53): First of these is that we need to build some of our own AI tech, and we focus on building the AI tech that we have the biggest advantage in that we have the most data that we can put into it, the most insights, the most criticality to our product and our business. So we have teams building our own AI models around design and images and that stuff. Second pillar is just finding the world's best AI people to partner with. And there's a whole bunch of stuff that you don't need to internalize in your company. You don't need to create an LLM because it's a commodity thing now. And there's a bunch of providers who can do it way better and have way more resources to do it with than you do. So finding a great partner like OpenAI, and we partnered with RunwayML to do video generation, finding the world's best and bringing them into your product with a great integration, the second pillar. (00:57:48): And for us, the third pillar is our app ecosystem. So we're fortunate now we've got 170 million people using the product every single month. We have quite an audience that people want access to. And through our app developer ecosystem, they can build apps which directly integrate with the Canva product to give them access to those hundreds of millions of people when people are quite eager to do that. Now, we've seen huge uptake in that from AI developers who have included stuff in Canva from music generators to virtual avatars that can present your presentation to you to a whole slew of things. And those three pillars have, I think, allowed us to create a really coherent experience and one that still keeps a focus on what people want to do, how to help them reach their big goals in a way that doesn't just push technology in the face in a way that just is part of the experience and is a natural way of getting them to where they want to go.
turns.zh: 作为科技公司，你永远得不断演进、用最好的技术。我们起步时，那是手机和云计算，是真正解锁 Canva 的创新。AI 是下一个十年的创新，是帮你做出更好产品的下一个关键技术——但它也不能只是你产品的基础。你不能只是做个纯粹架在 LLM 外面的“rapper”式的产品。你还是得想人们到底想做什么、怎么做出真正满足那个需求的产品。不是往一个已有的东西上糊个聊天机器人就完了，而是深层去思考 AI 怎么帮他们更快达到目标。我们把 AI 看成“设计民主化”的下一个方式——帮更多人设计、帮更多人更快设计、帮更多人以更好的质量更快设计。我们就是这么把 AI 放进 Canva 平台的每个角落的。（00:56:04）我们大概七年前就有了一支机器学习工程师团队。我觉得他们的工作现在视觉化多了，也更直面客户了——早些年他们只做邮件和首页里的推荐引擎、给你推模板。但现在他们能用一些超酷的技术，帮人们生成图片、做设计、总结文字、翻译成一百种语言，真的是能直接摆到客户面前的东西，特别让人兴奋。过去两年，我们在 Canva 里培养了越来越多视觉 AI 专家，我们通过三根支柱来把 AI 放进产品。（00:56:53）第一根：我们得自己建一部分 AI 技术，我们聚焦在我们有最大优势的那块……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was also looking at the GPT story of the fifth most popular custom GPT where people can generate logos using it. So maybe that's driving some growth too. I know you wanted to share something that you guys are launching or have launched by the time this episode comes out. Is that true?
turns.zh: 我还在看那个 GPT 的故事——第五受欢迎的自定义 GPT，人们能用它生成 logo。所以那可能也在带来一些增长。我知道你想分享点你们正在发布、或者在这期节目上线前已经发布的东西。是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Cameron Adams
turns.en: Yeah, so we've got a big event in Los Angeles in a couple of months. It's our Canva create, which is an evolution of the season openness that we used to do. So season openers are no longer just inside Canva now. We actually invite our whole community in, and we're going to have probably about 4,000 people in the theater in LA and a couple of million online. And we're really going to be pulling the covers off pretty much the next decade of Canva. We've focused for the first decade of Canva on unlocking individuals and small businesses, giving them the tools that they need to design and to express themselves and create visual content. And as Canva has grown and people have gotten used to creating this stuff, they've invited their teams in, they now collaborate with people on presentations, on Canva videos, on swag T-shirts that they need to make for their event next week. (01:00:06): And as more and more people are using Canva together, it's picking up a lot of steam. We've got 95% of the Fortune 500 using Canva. We've got huge teams of thousands of people using Canva. And this has really opened our eyes to not only the enterprise opportunity, but also just the way to redesign the way people work. And that is what the event at the end of May is about. It's really redesigning work for a whole number of different verticals, from marketing to sales to HR to IT to creatives that work inside large teams, large organizations, large enterprises. We've redesigned Canva for this collaborative enterprise age, so we'll be pulling the covers off that alongside work kits, which are a whole verticalized experiences for people inside marketing and sales and HR that want to use Canva, as well as a bunch of improvements to our AI products and an actual enterprise skew that we're launching as well. (01:01:13): So through this growth and through getting to understand the needs of CIOs and heads of security at enterprises, we've realized that there pretty much needs to be a new enterprise product of Canva that meets the needs of hugely scaled teams, which has been quite different for us because we have scaled from those individuals just using the product all by themselves and organically growing the teams. And now looking at it from a top-down lens and building that enterprise products is what we've been focused on for the last couple of years. So we'll be pulling the covers off that as well in LA.
turns.zh: 对，我们几个月后会在洛杉矶办一场大活动，是我们的 Canva Create，是以前“season openness”的进化版。所以现在不再是只在 Canva 内部做 season opener 了。我们会把整个社区都请进来，洛杉矶的剧院里大概会有 4000 人，线上还有几百万。我们会真的把 Canva 下一个十年的幕布拉开。Canva 的第一个十年，我们聚焦在解锁个人和小企业，给他们需要的工具去设计、表达自己、做视觉内容。随着 Canva 长大、人们习惯了做这些东西，他们把团队也拉了进来，现在一起在演示文稿、Canva 视频、为下周活动要做的周边 T 恤上协作。（01:00:06）越来越多人一起用 Canva，它越来越有势头。财富 500 强里 95% 在用 Canva。我们有几千人的大团队在用。这真的让我们睁了眼——不只是企业机会，还有重新设计人们工作方式的可能。这就是五月底那场活动的主题：为各种不同的垂直行业重新设计工作，从市场到销售到 HR 到 IT，到大型团队、大型组织、大型企业里的创意人。我们为这个协作的企业时代重新设计了 Canva，所以会揭开它的面纱，同时还有 work kits——给市场、销售、HR 里想用 Canva 的人的整套垂直化体验——还有一堆 AI 产品的改进，以及一个我们也在推的企业版。（01:01:13）所以通过这种增长、通过理解 CIO 和企业安全负责人的需求，我们意识到基本需要一个新的……
